text: Once a shared pipeline template is being called from fifty or three hundred repositories, that template repo has become a dependency exactly as real as any npm package those repos install. This lesson is about treating it that way — with semantic versioning and a changelog — so a breaking change doesn't silently break every consuming repo on the same day.

Here's what happens without that discipline. Someone edits the template to rename an input, pushes straight to main, and every repo still pointed at at-main breaks on its very next run, simultaneously, across the whole organization, with no warning at all. The fix is the same discipline that already exists for application dependencies: version numbers that actually mean something, and a rollout path a breaking change can travel instead of landing everywhere at once.

Semantic versioning maps onto a template the same way it maps onto a library's public API. A patch release is an internal fix that changes no input or output. A minor release adds something backward-compatible, like a new optional input with a sane default. A major release is a breaking change — renaming or removing an input, making a secret required that used to be optional, or changing a job name that a consumer's branch protection rule depends on.

Tagging every release precisely, while also keeping a moving v1 tag pointed at the latest 1.x release, gives consumers a real choice. A repo that calls at-v1 picks up every non-breaking improvement automatically. A repo that needs to freeze behavior entirely pins the exact v1.4.0 tag instead, and nobody is forced onto v2 until they deliberately change that one line in their own workflow file.

A changelog at the root of the template repo, updated with every tagged release, is the one artifact that lets a team self-serve the answer to whether it's safe to move from v1 to v2, without filing a support ticket. Keep it in the standard changelog shape: what's breaking, what's added, what's fixed, release by release.

Versioning solves half the problem — it stops a breaking change from landing on everyone unannounced. The other half is making sure the standards your organization actually cares about, required scans and required approvals, don't depend on every team remembering a policy page. Next lesson covers building those requirements into the template's own defaults instead.
